A second version has Rav Adda urging the separation.

answer.actor: A woman selling belts and a man
answer.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman, proposing betrothal if he gave it back; she took it silently.
answer.turn: Silence is ambiguous.
answer.outcome: Rav Nachman says she may claim she took her own property, so not betrothed.
answer.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man snatched one and asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it back. She took it and said nothing. Rav Nachman ruled she could say she was just taking her own property, so she is not betrothed.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi named Babylonian places and their sins, including Bireta DeSatya, who trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after excommunication.
answer.turn: Birth of Rav Yehuda was announced.
answer.outcome: No resolution; a list of prophetic remarks.
answer.summary: Dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi described Babylonian towns: one of Ammonites, one of mamzerim, one where brothers swapped wives, and one whose people trapped fish on Shabbat, were excommunicated and apostatized. He ended by saying a child, Adda bar Ahava, was circumcised and Rav Yehuda was born that day.
answer.missing: It is a list of prophecies more than a single story.

answer.actor: Ten men and a woman
answer.event: Ten men carried a woman out on a bier and had intercourse with her.
answer.outcome: Used as evidence for a halakhic rule.
answer.summary: Rav ruled that a woman may not be secluded even with ten immoral men. As evidence, there was an incident where ten men carried a woman out on a bier as if she were dead and abused her.
answer.missing: Only a one-line incident, cited as proof.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel and a groom
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found an unobstructed orifice.
answer.turn: Gamliel suggests he diverted his path and tells a parable of a man at a dark door.
answer.outcome: Unresolved; suggests the man's claim does not prove non-virginity.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel and said he had found his bride's orifice open. Gamliel asked if he had perhaps diverted, telling a parable of a man in the dark who finds a door open or locked depending on the angle. Another version says he asked if the man had intentionally diverted.

answer.actor: A man giving a conditional divorce
answer.event: A man said his betrothed would be divorced if he did not marry her by New Moon of Adar, then claimed he meant Nisan.
answer.turn: His claim creates doubt over the divorce.
answer.outcome: The Gemara notes the dispute of Abaye and Rava.
answer.summary: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, this would be a bill of divorce. When the date came he said he meant Nisan. The Gemara asks whether this raises a concern, and says it is a dispute of Abaye and Rava.
answer.missing: The case ends in a legal analysis.

answer.actor: Mar Zutra and Rabbi Yehuda from India
answer.event: Rabbi Yehuda, a convert without heirs, fell ill and Mar Zutra visited him.
answer.turn: Mar Zutra saw Yehuda was dying and told the slave to take his shoes home, claiming the slave.
answer.outcome: Yehuda died while Mar Zutra gained a slave.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda from India, a convert without heirs, grew ill and Mar Zutra visited. Seeing he was dying, Mar Zutra told Yehuda's slave to take his shoes to his house, acquiring the slave. One left to death and the other to life.

answer.actor: A woman and Rav Nachman
answer.event: A woman holding a bag of documents was claimed against by heirs; she said she seized it before the owner died.
answer.turn: Rav Nachman asks for witnesses and she has none.
answer.outcome: He rules it is seizure after death and void.
answer.summary: A woman held a bag of documents deposited with her. The heirs claimed it, but she said she had seized it while the owner lived. Rav Nachman asked for witnesses, and she had none, so he ruled it was seizure after death, which is nothing.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda
answer.event: Rav Yehuda ruled in a case of a husband feeding his wife's branches to his animals.
answer.outcome: Treated as consumption establishing possession.
answer.summary: The judges of Pumbedita say Rav Yehuda acted in a case of a bundle of branches, treating the husband's use as consumption of his wife's property, consistent with his rule on forbidden produce.
answer.missing: Only a thin report of a ruling.

answer.actor: Me'oret's slave
answer.event: Me'oret made her slave do three of the harmful acts and he died.
answer.turn: Raised as an objection to Abaye.
answer.outcome: Explained away as the slave being weak.
answer.summary: Abaye said the six acts kill in order, weaken out of order. Objection: Me'oret made her slave do three and he died. Answer: he was weak.
answer.missing: The anecdote is a single clause used in argument.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
answer.event: The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites in Rabbi's days.
answer.turn: Rabbi objects that no one can permit the altar's share.
answer.outcome: Implied: they remained forbidden.
answer.summary: In Rabbi's time the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites. Rabbi said that even if they permit the Jewish share, nobody can permit the altar's share.
answer.missing: Outcome only implied.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon helped his mother in and out of bed and boasted of honoring her in the study hall.
answer.turn: The scholars say he has not reached half of honor, since he never endured her throwing a purse into the sea.
answer.outcome: Rebuke stands.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could climb on and off her bed, and boasted of it in the study hall. They told him he had not reached half the required honor: had she thrown his purse into the sea in front of him, would he have avoided shaming her?

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
answer.event: Rabbi Yehoshua visited Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to study, found him among trees, and stretched a vine between them.
answer.turn: He asked about sowing near grapevines.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yochanan ruled permitted at ten cubits, forbidden beyond.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua went to study with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees. He stretched a vine from tree to tree and asked about sowing there. Rabbi Yochanan said it was permitted at ten cubits and forbidden beyond.

answer.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya
answer.event: A widow came before Rav Yosef asking for sustenance, wine and silk.
answer.turn: He asks why silk.
answer.outcome: She answers she needs it for him and his friends; implied she receives it.
answer.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef asking for sustenance and wine, and he granted both. She also asked for silk garments. When he asked why, she said it was so she would not be ashamed before him and his colleagues.
answer.missing: Whether silk was granted is implied.

answer.actor: A betrothed couple and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A betrothed man and pregnant woman came before Rav Yosef; she said it was his.
answer.turn: He admits it.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef rules no suspicion need be considered.
answer.summary: A betrothed couple came before Rav Yosef, she pregnant and saying he was the father. He admitted it. Rav Yosef said there was no reason for concern since he concedes it and the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
answer.missing: Passage cuts off mid-sentence; resolved in segment 5.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: A yavam and yevama who both admitted they had not consummated the levirate marriage came before Rava, who ordered halitza.
answer.turn: Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza.
answer.outcome: Rava conceded that if the baraita is taught, it stands, and retracted his ruling.
answer.summary: A couple who both said their levirate marriage was never consummated came before Rava, and he told the court to arrange halitza and settle the case. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires a bill of divorce as well as halitza. Rava answered that if that baraita is taught, then it stands, and he withdrew his ruling.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: When his daughter's husband Abba (Gamliel's brother) died childless, Rabban Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her rival wife.
answer.turn: The Gemara questions whether this proves anything, since Gamliel followed Beit Hillel, and then explains she was an aylonit.
answer.outcome: No firm outcome; the incident is only used as a proof and then explained away.
answer.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died childless, and Rabban Gamliel married her rival wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara first takes this as proof that rival wives of a daughter may do so, then notes Gamliel followed Beit Hillel and explains that the daughter was an aylonit, which changes the law.
answer.missing: The incident is a one-line precedent cited for a legal argument and has no development beyond it.
The passage cites a baraita about Michal and Jonah's wife only as a legal proof about time-bound mitzvot.

answer.actor: Rav Naḥman
answer.event: When Rav Naḥman came to Neharde'a he told the people to clear away the earth that had half-filled the entrances so the doors could be locked.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks whether this shows he thinks doors must be locked.
answer.outcome: It concludes he only required the doors to be fit for locking.
answer.summary: The entrances of Neharde'a had been filled halfway with earth. When Rav Naḥman arrived he ordered the earth cleared away so the doors could be locked. The Gemara debates what this shows and concludes it only means the doors must be fit to be locked.
answer.missing: The anecdote is a single instruction used as a legal proof, with no real action or resolution beyond the legal reading.

answer.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
answer.event: Captive women were lodged in his house with the ladder removed, and when one of them passed, he lifted a huge ladder alone and began climbing toward her.
answer.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself, braced his legs and shouted that there was a fire in Amram's house.
answer.outcome: The Sages came and he told them it is better to be shamed in this world; he made his evil inclination come out of him as a pillar of fire and told it he was still superior.
answer.summary: Captive women redeemed in Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's house with the ladder taken away. When one passed, her beauty lit up the opening, and Rav Amram lifted a ladder ten men could not move and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and shouted that there was a fire in his house, so the Sages came and saw him. He told them better to be shamed now than in the World-to-Come, and made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire, telling it that he, though flesh, had prevailed over fire.

answer.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Naḥman
answer.event: During a drought everyone in Neharde'a sold their mansions to buy wheat.
answer.turn: Wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
answer.outcome: Rav Naḥman ruled that the mansions be returned to their former owners.
answer.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold his mansion to buy wheat. In the end wheat arrived, making the sales unnecessary, and Rav Naḥman ruled that the mansions go back to their original owners.

answer.missing: The passage is a legal argument, with a short baraita quoted by Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok only as proof.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda bar Yeḥezkel
answer.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda in a Pumbedita butcher shop, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and proclaimed him a slave.
answer.turn: The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court, where Rav Yehuda showed his superiority, and the man himself arrived and boasted of Hasmonean descent.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda was vindicated by Rav Mattana's report of Shmuel; the man was publicized as a slave, marriage contracts were torn up, and Rav Yehuda escaped a stoning crowd by threatening to reveal their lineage.
answer.summary: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda over the meat queue in Pumbedita, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and declared him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court. Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Naḥman's speech and refused his hospitality on technical grounds, then the sides questioned his rulings until the man arrived claiming royal Hasmonean descent. Rav Mattana confirmed Shmuel's ruling that anyone claiming this is a slave, and the man was publicly branded. Many marriages were annulled, and when a mob pursued Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal their own lineage and they dropped the stones.

answer.actor: Rabba bar bar Ḥana and Rav
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Ḥana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
answer.turn: A baraita calls such an agent's conduct deceitful, so the Gemara asks how Rav could do it.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains that the local violent landowners respected Rav but not Rabba, and that Rav feared someone else would buy the land if he took time to inform him.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Ḥana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav went and bought it for himself. The Gemara asks how he could, and answers that the sellers were violent men who honored Rav but not Rabba, and that Rav feared someone else would buy it while he went to inform Rabba.

answer.missing: The passage describes a yard in Pum Nahara only as the setting for Abaye and Rava's legal proposals about side posts.
The exchange is a halakhic argument between Rav Dimi and Abaye, with only a moment of silence and a compliment as incident.

answer.actor: Shmuel
answer.event: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry and then said he had a case before him.
answer.turn: The favor created a bond between them.
answer.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from judging the man's case.
answer.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a narrow ferry when a man gave him a hand to help him out. Shmuel asked what he was doing there, and the man said he had a case for him to judge. Shmuel said he was disqualified, because the man had done him a favor.

answer.missing: The passage is a single piece of health advice from Elijah to Rabbi Natan, with no event.

answer.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the Land.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar mourned that he died in an unclean land, and when told his coffin was being brought to the Land, said it is not the same as being absorbed by its soil while alive.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar maintained that burial in the Land does not undo dying outside it.
answer.summary: Ulla often ascended to Eretz Yisrael but died outside it. When Rabbi Elazar was told, he said the verse about dying in an unclean land was fulfilled through him. They told him Ulla's coffin was coming for burial in the Land, but he answered that being absorbed by its soil while alive is not the same as after death.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: Their boat set sail on Shabbat; Gamliel and Elazar ben Azarya walked its whole length while Yehoshua and Akiva stayed within four cubits.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks what the sages' stringency implies about whether the boat was moving.
answer.outcome: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak uses it to argue that they did not disagree about a moving boat.
answer.summary: Several sages traveling from Pelandarsin found their boat out at sea on Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked around the whole boat, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva would not move beyond four cubits, choosing to be stringent. The Gemara uses the incident only as evidence in a legal argument.
answer.missing: The incident is quoted for its legal implication and has no ending beyond the sages' differing behavior.
The passage is Rabbi Zeira's report of a ruling he heard from Rabbi Asi in Eretz Yisrael, a legal citation rather than an event.

answer.actor: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba
answer.event: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi as they studied, and they stood for him.
answer.turn: He told them they need not, since they were ordained and he was not, and since the Torah does not stand before its students.
answer.outcome: He released them from the obligation to stand.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying Torah when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed, and they stood up. He told them they did not have to, because they were ordained scholars and he was not, and because someone engaged in Torah study need not stand.

answer.actor: Rav Anan
answer.event: After Rav Anan's act caused a miscarriage of justice, Elijah, who used to visit him to teach Seder deEliyahu, departed.
answer.turn: Rav Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah returned, but now appeared in frightening forms.
answer.outcome: Rav Anan made a box, sat in it before Elijah, and learned the whole Seder, which is why there are a Major and a Minor Seder.
answer.summary: Elijah used to visit Rav Anan and teach him the Seder deEliyahu. After Rav Anan's action led to a miscarriage of justice, Elijah left, and Rav Anan fasted and prayed until he returned, but then Elijah frightened him in terrifying forms. Rav Anan made a box, sat inside it before Elijah, and learned the whole Seder, which explains the Major Order taught before the incident and the Minor Order after.

answer.actor: A brewer
answer.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from the date beer he was making for someone else, and the owner told him to give her sharper sediment of better quality.
answer.turn: The brewer asked Rava whether the owner's remark meant he had relinquished his rights.
answer.outcome: Rava told him the owner's words applied only to teruma, so the woman was not betrothed.
answer.summary: A brewer making date beer for someone betrothed a woman with its sediment. The owner found him and told him to use a sharper, better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner had given up his rights, and Rava said no: such a remark counts only for teruma, so the sediment was still the owner's.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami
answer.event: A man deposited seven pearls in Rabbi Meyasha's house, and Rabbi Meyasha died without saying whose they were.
answer.turn: His family and the depositor disputed ownership before Rabbi Ami.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, because Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy enough to own them and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at Rabbi Meyasha's house, and Rabbi Meyasha died without saying who owned them. His family and the depositor came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled for the depositor. He reasoned that Rabbi Meyasha was not rich enough to own such gems and that the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives and Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow for a debt and Rabbi Yohanan approved, but Reish Lakish ordered it returned.
answer.turn: Reish Lakish overruled Rabbi Yohanan's approval, and the relatives went back to complain.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing because his peer disagreed with him.
answer.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized a cow belonging to orphans, whose father owed them money. Rabbi Yohanan said they had seized it properly, but Reish Lakish told them to give it back. When they returned to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could not help, since his equal disagreed with him.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman and the daughter of his relative
answer.event: Purchasers of a dead woman's marriage-contract rights claimed the money from her daughter, and Rav Nahman suggested a way for the daughter to avoid paying.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman's advice: forgive her father's marriage-contract debt so she could inherit it from him.
answer.outcome: The daughter heard this, went and forgave her father's obligation as advised.
answer.summary: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her marriage contract rights, was divorced and then died. The buyers claimed the money from her daughter. Rav Nahman asked aloud whether no one would advise the girl to forgive her father's obligation and then inherit from him. She heard and did exactly that.

answer.actor: A couple, their minor daughter, and the father's relative
answer.event: A couple disagreed over whom to marry their minor daughter to; the father yielded to the mother's relative, but during the festive meal his own relative came up to the roof and betrothed her.
answer.turn: The father's relative betrothed the girl in the middle of the meal.
answer.outcome: The passage itself ends with the betrothal; whether it is valid is only addressed in the following discussion (presumed not valid).
answer.summary: A father wanted to marry off his minor daughter to his relative and the mother to hers. Under pressure the father agreed to the mother's relative. While they were eating and drinking, the father's relative came onto the roof and betrothed her. The Gemara then assumes the father did not desire this betrothal.
answer.missing: The legal outcome of the betrothal is stated only in the surrounding discussion.

answer.actor: Mar Zutra
answer.event: Mar Zutra compelled a rebellious wife who said she was disgusted with her husband to stay with him.
answer.turn: A son, Rabbi Hanina of Sura, was born of this couple, which suggests coercion can bring blessing.
answer.outcome: The Gemara rejects this as a precedent: the good result was due to heavenly assistance.
answer.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband, saying she was disgusted with him, and Mar Zutra forced her to stay. From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara says this proves nothing general; it happened by heavenly help.

answer.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract rights, and Rami bar Hama and Rava
answer.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, saying he would not reimburse if she objected; she died without objecting, then he himself contested the sale.
answer.turn: Rami bar Hama thought he stands in his mother's place and can object; Rava challenged this.
answer.outcome: Rava argued he guaranteed against his own objections too; the passage is essentially a legal exchange.
answer.summary: A man sold his mother's marriage contract rights on the condition that he would not compensate if she objected. She died having never objected, and he came and contested the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he could object as her proxy, but Rava answered that he had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
answer.missing: No judgment is explicitly delivered; it is framed as a legal argument.

answer.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether the son would become angry.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks whether this tempted the son to sin and violated the ban on destruction.
answer.outcome: The outcome of the test is not stated; the following discussion only defends the act's permissibility.
answer.summary: Rav Huna decided to tear silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would get angry. The Gemara then raises objections that this might make the son sin or destroy property, and answers them. How Rabba actually reacted is never told.
answer.missing: How the son reacted.

answer.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern (per Rabbi Meir)
answer.event: Rabbi Meir cites an incident of a man falling into the Great Cistern, which the Sages say is a miracle not to be used for halakha.
answer.turn: Debate over whether surviving without eating, drinking or sleeping makes it miraculous.
answer.outcome: The incident itself is only gestured at; the passage is about whether it counts as miraculous.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir mentions an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and survived. The Sages answer that one does not cite miraculous events. The Gemara then debates what exactly was miraculous about the case.
answer.missing: The incident's actual details are not told in the text shown.

answer.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
answer.event: Their mother wrote her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening, and each brother got a different judge to confirm his claim.
answer.turn: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman, who had ruled differently, confronted each other about their reasons.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman rejected Rav Sheshet's reasoning, saying he himself is a judge and Rav Sheshet is not, and that Rav Sheshet's reasoning was originally different.
answer.summary: A mother gave her property by deed to Rami bar Hama in the morning and to his brother Mar Ukva in the evening. Rami won before Rav Sheshet and Mar Ukva won before Rav Nahman. When Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman, they argued over whose reasoning held up, and Rav Nahman insisted his was the judge's discretion while Rav Sheshet was no judge.

answer.actor: A launderer who visited Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi every day
answer.event: After a Divine Voice promised the World-to-Come to all who attended Rabbi's funeral, the launderer, who had not come that day, heard of the death and the promise.
answer.turn: Overcome with grief, he climbed to the roof and fell to his death.
answer.outcome: A Divine Voice declared that this launderer too is destined for the World-to-Come.
answer.summary: On the day of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's funeral a Divine Voice said all who attended would have a place in the World-to-Come. A launderer who visited Rabbi daily had not come that day. When he heard, he went up to the roof and fell to the ground and died, and a Divine Voice announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

answer.actor: A man who had never been married and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man came before Rav Nahman claiming he found an unobstructed opening on his wedding night.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman suspected he had experience with prostitutes since he was unmarried.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
answer.summary: A man who had not been married before told Rav Nahman that he had found his bride's opening unobstructed. Rav Nahman said to flog him with palm branches, since prostitutes are common around him, so he must have learned of the condition from experience.

answer.actor: Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana
answer.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi if he remembered testimony; Rav Ashi said no, but after being reminded eventually remembered and testified for him.
answer.turn: Rav Kahana was hesitant that he had influenced Rav Ashi's memory.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi said he was not relying on Rav Kahana but had made an effort and truly remembered.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi knew testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. At first Rav Ashi said he did not remember, but eventually he recalled it and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana doubtful about it, Rav Ashi told him he was not relying on him but had made an effort and remembered on his own.

answer.actor: Rav Avya
answer.event: Rav Avya came to Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed.
answer.turn: He ruled that the door may not be locked on Shabbat with such a bolt.
answer.outcome: Only his ruling is given; no further events.
answer.summary: Rav Avya visited Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed. He declared that this door could not be locked on Shabbat. The text gives no reaction or aftermath.
answer.missing: What the man did in response.

answer.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon and the Sages
answer.event: The Sages set aside four hundred gold coins for her perfume account for a single day.
answer.turn: She responded by blessing them: may you set the same for your own daughters.
answer.outcome: They answered Amen.
answer.summary: After the death of her husband, the Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for her daily perfume expenses. She said to them that they should set the same for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

answer.actor: The tumtum of Biri
answer.event: Rabbi Ami cites a tumtum of Biri who was seated and torn open and then fathered seven children, as an objection to Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehuda's answer: check where his children came from.
answer.outcome: The case is used only as an argument and the outcome is not narrated beyond the seven children.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ami raised the case of a tumtum from Biri, who was seated, torn open and later fathered seven children, to challenge Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda could reply that one should look into where those children came from.
answer.missing: The incident is only an offhand reference within a legal challenge.

answer.actor: Shmuel's father and Shmuel's daughters
answer.event: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women and Shmuel objected; later Shmuel's own daughters were taken captive.
answer.turn: The daughters left their captors outside, declared in the study hall that they were captive and pure, and were permitted to marry.
answer.outcome: When the captors then came in, the permission stood, and it became clear they were Shmuel's daughters.
answer.summary: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women who had come to Neharde'a, and Shmuel questioned him; the father asked whether he would treat his own daughters so. It came true: Shmuel's daughters were captured and brought to Eretz Yisrael. They entered the study hall first and each declared she was captive and pure, and were permitted. When their captors came in, it was revealed whose daughters they were.

answer.actor: A certain woman and the guard she was with
answer.event: A woman, visiting her husband's grave, had intercourse with a man guarding an executed body, then suggested they disinter her husband so he could claim the guarded body was safe.
answer.turn: Even in acute mourning she succumbed to temptation.
answer.outcome: She removed her husband's body from its grave.
answer.summary: The Rabbis' view is illustrated by an incident of a woman who removed her husband's body from the grave. She had gone to his grave, been with a man guarding a hanged body, and when that body was stolen proposed that her husband be dug up to stand in for it.
answer.missing: The Aramaic only hints at the story; the details come from the translator's explanation.

answer.actor: Rabbi Meir and a man who made an eiruv with onions
answer.event: Rabbi Meir spent Shabbat in Ardiska and a man told him he had made an eiruv with onions in order to walk to Tiv'in.
answer.turn: Rabbi Meir did not accept the onion eiruv.
answer.outcome: He made the man stay within his four cubits.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir was spending Shabbat in Ardiska when a man told him he had made an eiruv of Shabbat limits with onions to reach Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir would not accept it and kept him within four cubits.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, and his sharecropper
answer.event: The sharecropper brought a basket of fruit on Thursday instead of Friday because he had a lawsuit before Rabbi Yishmael.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, disqualified himself, and had others judge the case.
answer.outcome: While the case was judged he kept thinking of ways the sharecropper could win, and concluded that bribe-takers must be even more biased.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper normally brought fruit on Friday but once came on Thursday, because he had a case before the rabbi. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself, and two scholars judged the case. All the while he found himself mentally arguing for the sharecropper, and reflected that if he felt this way without taking anything, bribe-takers must be far more biased.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins, and Rava
answer.event: A man grabbed coins from someone, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed.
answer.turn: He came before Rava to ask about her status.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal ineffective, since the coins were stolen and the owner presumably has not despaired of them.
answer.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man snatched coins from another person, threw them to her, and said she was betrothed to him. He asked Rava about it. Rava ruled it was not valid because the coins were not truly his, as the owner would not have given up on them.

answer.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee
answer.event: They bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks what is remarkable about a litra of meat, so the story is read as extravagant giving.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna and Rav Ashi explain how costly it was, but the incident itself has no ending.
answer.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee once bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of good family from Tzippori. The Gemara asks why this is remarkable. Rav Huna says the meat was expensive poultry or bought at a very high price. Rav Ashi says that in a tiny village they slaughtered a whole animal for him each day.
answer.missing: The incident is a bare report of a practice with no complication or resolution; most of the passage is explanation of its extravagance.

answer.actor: A woman holding a bag of deposited documents
answer.event: The heirs of the depositor demanded the bag, and she said she had seized it from him while he was alive to collect a debt.
answer.turn: Rav Nachman asked for witnesses that the deceased had claimed it from her and she refused to hand it over, and she had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled it was seizure after death, which is worth nothing, so the heirs get the documents.
answer.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the heirs of the depositor came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him in his lifetime because he owed her money. Before Rav Nachman she could not produce witnesses that he had demanded it and she had refused. He ruled that her seizure counted as one made after death, which is invalid, so the heirs prevailed.

answer.actor: Rabbi Helbo
answer.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite; he had no answer and asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.
answer.turn: Rabbi Helbo could not answer the question himself.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha supplied a ranked list of who reads next.
answer.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite. He did not have the answer, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Rabbi Yitzchak answered with an order of readers, starting with scholars appointed as communal leaders and ending with any person.
answer.missing: The passage itself holds only the opening of the question; the rest of the exchange is in the following context segment. It is a thin question-and-answer exchange with little incident.

answer.actor: Ameimar
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for her one-tenth dowry share of her father's estate, and her brothers said that if they had the money they would pay her off in cash.
answer.turn: The brothers' offer to pay cash contradicted Ameimar's view that she is an heir, and he said nothing.
answer.outcome: His silence was taken to show that he retracted and agreed she is a creditor who can be paid off in cash.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for one-tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers told her that if they had the cash they would pay her off with money. Ameimar heard this and said nothing, and from that silence it was concluded that he had abandoned his view and treated her as a creditor.
answer.missing: The passage opens with Rav Ashi's legal position, which is argument rather than narrative.

answer.actor: Rav Acha bar Abba
answer.event: He visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and put his granddaughter on his lap.
answer.turn: Rav Chisda objected that she might be betrothed, and Rav Acha countered that Rav Chisda had himself broken Rav's rule; Rav Chisda then said Rav Acha broke Shmuel's rule against using a woman.
answer.outcome: Rav Acha answered with another statement of Shmuel that such acts done for the sake of Heaven are permitted.
answer.summary: Rav Acha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Chisda asked whether he did not think she might already be betrothed. They traded accusations of ignoring the rulings of Rav and Shmuel. Rav Acha finished by citing Shmuel that such things are permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.

answer.actor: Dama ben Netina
answer.event: He was wearing a golden cloak and sitting among Roman nobles when his mother tore it from him, slapped his head and spat in his face.
answer.turn: He was publicly humiliated by his own mother.
answer.outcome: He did not embarrass her in return.
answer.summary: Dama ben Netina once sat among the nobles of Rome wearing a golden cloak. His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck him on the head and spat in his face. He did not shame her in return.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yosef ruled in a case following Rav and Shmuel took offense, saying wisdom is not measured out in large measure only to this sage.
answer.turn: Shmuel's anger is used as evidence that Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
answer.outcome: The Gemara suggests Rav Yosef may have ruled in a case where the woman denied her father's right, so even Shmuel would agree.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of Dabil, once decided a case in line with Rav, and Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom is measured in a large measure only for this sage. The Gemara uses the anecdote to argue about whether Rav and Shmuel really disagreed.
answer.missing: The anecdote is only a brief proof within a legal argument; the details of the case Rav Yosef decided are absent.

answer.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract
answer.event: He sold rights to his mother's ketubah, stipulating he would not reimburse the buyer if she objected; his mother died without objecting, and then he himself contested the sale.
answer.turn: He tried to void the sale on his own, and Rami bar Chama thought he stood in his mother's place.
answer.outcome: Rava rejected this, since he took on responsibility against his own objection even if not his mother's.
answer.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract and told the buyer he would not compensate him if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he came and contested the sale himself. Rami bar Chama thought he could, standing in her place. Rava replied that he had at least guaranteed the sale against his own objections.

answer.actor: Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara
answer.event: They disagreed over whether a non-priest who served on Shabbat is liable on two counts or one, and each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he heard his view from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; the same happened again in two further cases.
answer.turn: Both swore contradictory oaths about the same teacher's words, which forced the question of how both could be honest.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explores explanations and ends with an unresolved difficulty before offering a possible resolution in later context.
answer.summary: Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed over whether a non-priest who served in the Temple on Shabbat is liable on two counts or one. Each leapt up and swore by the Temple service that he heard his answer from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then each reasoned out his view. The same pair repeated the oath-swearing in two similar disputes. The text then turns to analysing how both could be telling the truth.
answer.missing: The passage is mostly legal reasoning; the oath scenes recur and no resolution is within the segments, and most segments listed are the argument paired with the oaths.

answer.actor: Rav
answer.event: Rav arrived at Apsetaya and prohibited its residents from climbing a tree stripped of its branches.
answer.turn: This seemed to contradict a ruling that it is permitted.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav found an unguarded field and fenced it in with a stringency.
answer.summary: Rav once came to a place called Apsetaya and forbade climbing even a tree that had been stripped of its branches. This seemed to contradict the permission the Gemara had just established. The Gemara explains that Rav found a place where transgression was widespread and added a safeguard.
answer.missing: It is only a brief precedent cited in a legal discussion, with no scene or detail of Rav's visit.

answer.actor: Rami bar Yechezkel
answer.event: He came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees with honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats mixing together.
answer.turn: He recognised the sight as the fulfilment of the verse about a land flowing with milk and honey.
answer.outcome: He declared that this is the meaning of the verse.
answer.summary: Rami bar Yechezkel happened to come to Benei Berak. He saw goats grazing beneath fig trees, honey oozing from the figs and milk dripping from the goats, the two mixing together. He said that this is what the verse means by a land flowing with milk and honey.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zeira and Rava
answer.event: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mechoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and Rava later taught there in sequence that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and then a mamzeret.
answer.turn: The first teaching enraged the many converts, who pelted Rabbi Zeira with etrogim; Rava's first teaching won him honour, but his second teaching made them say he had spoiled it.
answer.outcome: Rava defended himself by saying he had given converts the freedom to marry either kind of woman.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mechoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with their etrogim because converts took it as an insult. Rava first taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he then taught the mamzeret ruling, they said he had thrown away his earlier honour. He replied that he had done what was good for them, since converts could choose either way.

answer.actor: Rafram and Rav Ashi
answer.event: In a case like the preceding one, Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to give a firm ruling.
answer.turn: Under that pressure Rav Ashi decided the matter.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi collected the full value of the promissory note.
answer.summary: There was an incident like the one under discussion, and Rafram pressured Rav Ashi to rule definitively. Rav Ashi then collected the full value of the debt document, treating the damage as that of a ruined beam meant for a sculpture.
answer.missing: The facts of the incident, the parties and the case are not given; it is a one-line precedent.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yochanan
answer.event: Rabbi Abbahu stood in a bathhouse supported by two slaves when it collapsed, and Rabbi Yochanan went up stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi when the stair collapsed.
answer.turn: Each collapse should have dropped him, but each held on.
answer.outcome: Each saved himself and pulled his two supporters up with him; asked why he then needed support, Rabbi Yochanan said he was saving his strength for old age.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was in a bathhouse leaning on two slaves when it collapsed. He grabbed a pillar, climbed out and pulled both of them up. Rabbi Yochanan went up stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, and when the stairs gave way he climbed up and hauled them both along. When the Sages asked why he needed support if he was so strong, he said he was saving his strength for old age.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda
answer.event: He found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the entrance to Rabba's study hall and raised a contradiction between two baraitot of Rabbi Shimon.
answer.turn: They were silent and had no answer.
answer.outcome: They brought the problem to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved it by saying the first baraita concerned an animal found to be a tereifa.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel standing at Rabba's study hall and told them a baraita that seemed to imply Rabbi Shimon allowed benefit from animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. He then set a contradicting baraita against it, and they had no reply. They went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction by limiting the first case to a tereifa.

answer.actor: A buyer of one of two small plots of land
answer.event: A man with a hundred-dinar debt sold two small plots for fifty each, the creditor repossessed one and then came to repossess the other, and the purchaser took a hundred dinars to the creditor offering it to him.
answer.turn: The creditor sought the second plot after taking the first; the purchaser offered to pay the debt in cash.
answer.outcome: The outcome is not told in the passage.
answer.summary: A man owed a creditor a hundred dinars and sold two small plots for fifty each. The creditor repossessed one plot and then came for the other. The purchaser took a hundred dinars to him and said that if the plot was worth a hundred to him, fine, otherwise he should take the money and give up both plots.
answer.missing: How the creditor responded is not stated in the text shown; it is only implied by later context about the repossession document.

answer.actor: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan
answer.event: While traveling outside Eretz Yisrael, they twice saw a man sowing mixed kinds and one proposed ostracizing him.
answer.turn: The other sage rebuffed him each time, saying he did not understand the laws (the first case is permitted outside Eretz Yisrael; the second does not meet Rabbi Yoshiya's standard of sowing wheat, barley and a grape seed in one motion).
answer.outcome: The man was not ostracized.
answer.summary: Two sages walking on a road saw a man planting mixed seeds. One said they should ostracize him, but the other told him he did not understand the law, since this is not forbidden outside Eretz Yisrael. They then saw a man planting wheat and barley among vines and the same exchange followed, with the second sage citing Rabbi Yoshiya to show the man had not sown in the forbidden way. Neither man was ostracized.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel and a man who came before him
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he had found an open orifice (no sign of virginity) and Rabban Gamliel answered with a parable.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested the man had perhaps diverted his approach, comparing him to a man in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves the bolt.
answer.summary: A man came before Rabban Gamliel and said he had found an open orifice. Rabban Gamliel asked whether he had perhaps diverted his approach and told a parable of a man in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves it. A second version has Rabban Gamliel suggest the man did it intentionally. No result for the man is given.
answer.missing: How the case ended; what happened to the man or his claim.

answer.actor: Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law
answer.event: She seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
answer.turn: The Sages found they had no power to remove it from her.
answer.outcome: She kept the coins.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported an incident in which Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance. The Sages could not take it from her, so she kept it.
answer.missing: Any detail beyond a one-line report; it is cited only as legal precedent.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl, and Ravina
answer.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace and Ravina ruled on it.
answer.turn: Ravina held the degrading manner of betrothal removed any concern that her father consented.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled the betrothal is not a concern, meaning it is not valid.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl, without her father's consent, using a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace. Ravina ruled that even those who suspect the father may have consented do so only when the betrothal is done respectfully, and this was degrading, so it did not take effect.
answer.missing: The people involved, and any real narrative beyond the case and ruling.

answer.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: The Amorite asked how many dates the resident gathers from a palm tree by the Jordan.
answer.turn: The Amorite boasted they used to get 120 kor, twice the resident's 60, blaming the Israelites for ruining the land.
answer.outcome: The resident replied that he was only describing one side of the tree.
answer.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much he gathered from a palm tree on the Jordan's bank. The resident said sixty kor. The Amorite said the Israelites had ruined the land, since his people got 120. The resident answered that he had only counted one side of the tree.

answer.actor: A creditor, the orphans' herdsman and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox of orphans and the herdsman disputed when he seized it.
answer.turn: Each side told a different story about whether the seizure was before or after the debtor's death; Rav Nahman asked for witnesses and the herdsman had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the creditor could claim he seized it while the debtor was alive, so the seizure stood.
answer.summary: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman of some orphans. The creditor said he took it while the debtor was alive, while the herdsman said it was after death. They went to Rav Nahman, who found the herdsman had no witnesses. He held that since the creditor could claim to have bought it, he could equally claim to have seized it in the debtor's lifetime, so the claim stood.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A groom told him he found no blood on his wedding night and the bride said she was still a virgin.
answer.turn: Rabbi saw they were starving in a drought, so he had them bathed and fed, and sent them back to the room.
answer.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to take possession of his acquisition, quoting Lamentations about their shriveled skin.
answer.summary: During a famine a couple came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi because the groom found no blood. Rabbi saw their faces were dark from hunger, so he had them bathed, fed and given drink and then sent them into a room. This time the groom found blood and Rabbi told him to go take his bride, quoting a verse about skin shriveled on the bones.

answer.actor: Abaye
answer.event: Abaye rode his donkey along the riverbank and Rav Mesharshiyya and the rabbis on the other bank did not stand for him.
answer.turn: Abaye asked whether he was not their primary teacher.
answer.outcome: They answered that it had not occurred to them and that they had not seen him.
answer.summary: Abaye was riding a donkey along the Sagya River and the rabbis sitting on the other bank did not stand for him. He asked whether he was not their primary teacher, who must be honored from afar. They said they had not noticed him at all.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl, and Ravina
answer.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace and Ravina ruled on it.
answer.turn: Ravina held that the degrading manner removed any concern the father consented.
answer.outcome: The betrothal is not a concern, meaning it does not take effect.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl, without her father's consent, with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace. Ravina said that even those who suspect the father consented only apply that to a dignified betrothal, and this one was degrading, so there is no concern.
answer.missing: Who the man was, and anything beyond the case and its ruling.

answer.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya whose brother's widow fell to him for levirate marriage, and his brother
answer.event: The brother wanted to disqualify the yevama from him with a bill of divorce.
answer.turn: The man offered to share the inheritance; the brother feared he would be cheated as in the Pumbedita swindler story.
answer.outcome: The man offered to let the brother divide the property right away.
answer.summary: A man in Mata Mehasya had a yevama fall to him, and his brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce. The man asked if it was about the estate and promised to split it. The brother feared he would be cheated like the swindler from Pumbedita. The man then offered to let him divide the property from that moment.
answer.missing: The earlier Pumbedita story it refers to; whether the brother accepted.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama and Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina declined the headship of the yeshiva out of respect for the older Rabbi Afes and sat outside, with Levi studying beside him.
answer.turn: Rabbi Afes died and Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, leaving Levi with no one to study with.
answer.outcome: Levi traveled to Babylonia, where Rav, hearing of his limping teaching, deduced what had happened.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi appointed Hanina bar Hama to head the yeshiva, but he declined because Rabbi Afes was older. Afes sat at the head and Hanina sat outside, with Levi studying alongside him. When Afes died and Hanina took the head seat, Levi had no one to study with and went to Babylonia. There the people described a limping great man to Rav, who understood from his ruling what had happened.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined it before Rav.
answer.turn: He checked whether it was worth a peruta, and the Gemara then asked whether a worthless bundle fails to betroth, given Shmuel's opinion.
answer.outcome: The betrothal stands only if it was worth a peruta, the question being resolved by distinguishing certain from uncertain betrothal.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta, ruling she was betrothed if so and not if not. The Gemara then reconciled this with Shmuel's view by distinguishing certain from doubtful betrothal.
answer.missing: The result for the man and woman; it is mostly a legal ruling.

answer.actor: A man who rented a donkey, and the renter
answer.event: The owner warned the renter not to take the river path, but he went that way and the donkey died.
answer.turn: The renter came before Rava and admitted going by the river but said there was no water; Abaye objected that the claim cannot be accepted where there are witnesses.
answer.outcome: Rava accepted the renter's claim under the principle 'why would I lie', while Abaye disagreed.
answer.summary: A man rented out a donkey and told the renter to avoid the Pekod River path because of water, but the renter went that way and the donkey died. Before Rava, the renter admitted taking that path but said there was no water. Rava accepted his claim since he could have lied and said he took the other path. Abaye objected that this does not apply where witnesses know there is water.

answer.actor: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, and Rabbi Yannai
answer.event: Yehuda studied in the study hall and came home every Shabbat eve with a pillar of fire going before him.
answer.turn: One day he was absorbed in his learning and did not come, and Rabbi Yannai, seeing no pillar of fire, concluded he had died.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yannai said to turn his bed over, his words became like an error from a ruler, and Yehuda died.
answer.summary: Yehuda, a son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, came home each Shabbat eve and Rabbi Yannai would see a pillar of fire go before him. One day Yehuda was absorbed in study and did not come. Rabbi Yannai, seeing no sign, said to turn Yehuda's bed over as for a mourner, and that speech took effect and Yehuda died.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa
answer.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand before him.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: At the wedding of his son Abba Mar, Rav Pappa served drinks to the guests. He poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda, who did not stand before him. Rav Pappa became angry.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and his students, including Rabbi Yehuda
answer.event: A yevama came to perform halitza before Rabbi Tarfon, who told the onlookers to answer along with the court.
answer.outcome: The students recited the phrase three times, as instructed; nothing further is told.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalls sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to call out the verse's phrase three times. It is a brief anecdote used to illustrate a rule, with no real turn.
answer.missing: No complication or resolution; the anecdote only illustrates a practice.

answer.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
answer.event: Mar Ukva secretly tossed coins to a poor neighbor each day; the day the poor man came to see who it was, Mar Ukva and his wife fled and hid in a furnace.
answer.turn: His feet were scorched in the still-hot furnace while hers were not, and his wife offered her unburned feet to him.
answer.outcome: He was distraught, and she explained that her charity was more immediately helpful because she gave food from the home, so she was spared.
answer.summary: Mar Ukva used to toss four dinars to a poor neighbor every day without being seen. One day the poor man waited to find out who it was, and Mar Ukva and his wife ran away and hid in a furnace whose fire was banked but still hot. His feet were burned, and his wife told him to rest them on hers; when he was upset, she explained that her aid reaches the poor more directly than his money does.

answer.actor: Rav Giddel, Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Zeira and Rav Yitzhak Nappaha
answer.event: Rabbi Abba bought a piece of land that Rav Giddel was in the middle of acquiring, and Rav Giddel complained through Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival; Rabbi Abba pleaded ignorance and refused to sell, offering the land only as a gift.
answer.outcome: Rav Giddel would not accept a gift and Rabbi Abba would not use the land since Rav Giddel had been working on it, so it stayed untouched and was called the land of the Sages.
answer.summary: Rav Giddel was working to buy a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it first. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival with a parable of a poor man's loaf being snatched. Rabbi Abba said he hadn't known and would not sell, only give it as a gift. Rav Giddel refused gifts and Rabbi Abba felt he could not take the land, so it stayed unused and became known as the land of the Sages.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
answer.event: A man brought him the first shearing of his flock while having a lawsuit pending before him; Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself from the case.
answer.turn: While two other scholars judged the case, he found himself mentally arguing both sides for the litigant.
answer.outcome: He concluded that if he, who took nothing, was biased, then bribe-takers are certainly biased, and exclaimed against them.
answer.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing of his sheep. When the man admitted he also had a case, Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself, seating two other scholars to judge it. As he came and went he caught himself thinking up arguments for the man, and concluded that if he was swayed without taking anything, those who really take bribes are certainly corrupted.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A case about an alleyway closed by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before him, and he gave no ruling either way.
answer.outcome: He said neither permitted nor prohibited; the Gemara explains his silence.
answer.summary: An alleyway had the sea at one end and a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether it counted as enclosed was brought to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He declined to rule either way, because the dump might be removed or the sea might recede, though the partitions currently stood.
answer.missing: The case is cited as a precedent; no actors, no event beyond a non-ruling.

answer.actor: Rav Ashi
answer.event: At the king's gate, Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra's face go pale with craving for the food the chief butler carried past, and fed him some of it by finger.
answer.turn: The butler protested that Rav Ashi had spoiled the king's meal, and Rav Ashi said the food was already defective and then pointed to the exact spot.
answer.outcome: The soldiers checked that spot and found a leprous infection; Rav Ashi explained he had seen a leprous spirit hovering over it.
answer.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at the king's gate as the king's chief butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra go pale with craving and put some of the food into his mouth, and the butler complained that the king's meal was ruined. Rav Ashi claimed the food was already unfit; when the first check found nothing he pointed to a spot, and the infection was found there. He said he had seen a leprous spirit over it.

answer.actor: Ameimar and Mar Ukva
answer.event: A man did a small favor for a judge (removed a feather from Ameimar's head; covered Mar Ukva's spittle) and then said he had a case before him.
answer.turn: The favor made each judge feel biased.
answer.outcome: Each judge disqualified himself from hearing the man's case.
answer.summary: While Ameimar was sitting in judgment, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it; when the man said he had a case, Ameimar disqualified himself. Likewise a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva, and when he said he had a case, Mar Ukva too recused himself.

answer.actor: A man whose mother had been taken captive, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A case came before Rabbi where a man casually mentioned that he and his mother had been captured and that his thoughts were on his mother whenever he went out for water or wood.
answer.turn: His offhand remark, not formal testimony, was treated as reliable that she had stayed with him and was not defiled.
answer.outcome: Rabbi allowed the mother to marry into the priesthood on the basis of his words.
answer.summary: A man, speaking offhandedly, said that when he and his mother were captive among gentiles he always kept his attention on her, even while drawing water or gathering wood. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted this incidental remark and permitted her to marry a priest.

answer.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
answer.event: A man whose brother's widow lived in Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go there to marry her.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hanina sharply answered that the brother had married a foreign woman and died.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina implied the man should not follow his brother out of Eretz Yisrael.
answer.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael was obligated in levirate marriage to his late brother's widow, who lived in Babylonia, and asked Rabbi Hanina if he could go down to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that his brother had married a Samaritan and died, thank God, and asked whether he wanted to follow him there. The man was in effect refused.

answer.missing: The passage is Rava's rule about judges fixing a location, plus a report that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna held halitza before five judges and the legal explanation; no event with a turn.

answer.actor: Ben Nappaha and the Sages
answer.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha and a case came before the Sages about whether he prohibited carrying in all of them.
answer.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his actual residence prohibits carrying.
answer.summary: A man named ben Nappaha had houses in five courtyards in Usha, and the Sages were asked whether this required an eiruv in each. They ruled that only the place where he actually lived prohibited carrying.
answer.missing: A bare legal precedent; no personal drama or turn.

answer.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin and Rabbi Ami
answer.event: They bought a maidservant for small coins, put up a piece of silver as collateral because they had no cash, and she then rose in price.
answer.turn: The sellers wanted out of the sale and the case went to Rabbi Ami.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled there was no payment and no valid collateral, so no sale took place.
answer.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant but, lacking the coins, left a silver piece as collateral. When her price went up the sellers backed out and they brought the dispute to Rabbi Ami, who ruled that neither coins nor collateral had been validly given, so they had not acquired her.

answer.actor: Rava Tosfa'a
answer.event: He ruled a child fit (not a mamzer) when a woman's husband went overseas and she gave birth after twelve months.
answer.turn: The Gemara challenges whose opinion he followed.
answer.outcome: The ruling is defended in the next segment as following the majority.
answer.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she bore a child after twelve months. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, and the Gemara asks how, since this follows a minority opinion about delayed births.
answer.missing: The case is only a halakhic precedent being challenged; the details of the woman and child are absent.

answer.actor: Bonyos and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi a measuring vessel said to be an ancient se'a, and Rabbi measured it.
answer.outcome: He found it held 217 eggs, which does not match known se'a measures.
answer.summary: Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a-measure from Na'usa, and Rabbi measured its capacity at 217 eggs.
answer.missing: The significance and any resolution of the mismatch; it is a measurement report.

answer.actor: Rav Sheshet and a man passing his father-in-law's house
answer.event: Rav Sheshet lashed a man who merely passed by his father-in-law's door.
answer.turn: The Gemara objects that mere passing should not be punished.
answer.outcome: It explains that this man was suspected with his mother-in-law.
answer.summary: A man passed by the entrance to his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The Gemara explains that he was rumored to be involved with his mother-in-law.
answer.missing: No detail of the incident beyond a legal precedent.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
answer.event: A groom claimed he found no blood on the wedding night, and the bride said she was a virgin; Rabban Gamliel had the cloth brought to him.
answer.turn: He soaked and washed the cloth and found drops of blood on it.
answer.outcome: He told the groom to go take his bride, since she was a virgin.
answer.summary: A groom came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi saying he had not found blood, while the bride insisted she was a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth, soaked and laundered it, and found drops of blood. He told the groom to go take his purchase.

answer.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages set aside four hundred gold coins for her perfume allowance for a single day.
answer.turn: She answered them with a wish that they should do the same for their own daughters.
answer.outcome: They responded Amen.
answer.summary: When the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon was granted four hundred gold coins for perfume for one day, she said to the Sages that they should pledge that for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

answer.actor: A debtor's buyer and a creditor
answer.event: A creditor repossessed one of two plots a debtor had sold, then came to repossess the second.
answer.turn: The purchaser of the second plot took one hundred dinars to the creditor and offered it in exchange for giving up both claims.
answer.outcome: The creditor's response is not shown here; the text moves to the legal question of what is written in the repossession document.
answer.summary: A man owed one hundred dinars and had sold two plots for fifty each. The creditor took one from its buyer, then came for the other. That buyer went to him with one hundred dinars and offered him the money to give up his claims on both.
answer.missing: What the creditor did in response.

answer.actor: A dying man, his heirs, and Rav Ashi
answer.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter and died leaving only two half-shares of palm trees, and the heirs wanted to give her those.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether people call two halves a palm tree; Rav Mordekhai relayed a tradition from Rava that they do.
answer.outcome: The heirs may fulfill the bequest with the two halves.
answer.summary: A man promised his daughter a palm tree but at death owned only two half-shares in different trees. Rav Ashi wondered whether that counts, and Rav Mordekhai relayed Rava's view that people call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give the halves.
answer.missing: Mostly a legal question; the daughter's reaction is not told.

answer.actor: A woman divorced by a bill closer to her than to him, and the rabbis
answer.event: A bill of divorce was closer to the woman than to the man and was then lost.
answer.outcome: After the husband died, they required her to perform halitza rather than rely on the lost bill.
answer.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a case where a bill of divorce had been closer to the woman and was lost; they still required halitza to be safe.
answer.missing: Only a one-line precedent with no details of the people.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: After a reservoir at Yavne was measured and found short of the ritual-bath minimum, Tarfon and Akiva disagreed over whether past immersions in it counted, and argued it out with parables and analogies.
answer.turn: Akiva offered a second line of reasoning (the bath's disqualification comes from itself, not from others) that answered Tarfon's analogy.
answer.outcome: Tarfon accepted Akiva's reasoning and said that whoever parts from him parts from life.
answer.summary: A reservoir in Yavne, presumed to hold the required amount, was measured and found deficient. Rabbi Tarfon declared the earlier immersions pure and Rabbi Akiva declared them impure, and each argued his case with a parable about a disqualified priest. Akiva's second argument won Tarfon over, and Tarfon told him that anyone who separates from him separates from life.

answer.actor: A man who rented out a millstone and the man who rented it
answer.event: A millstone owner who had been paid by the renter's grinding grew rich, bought his own millstone and donkey, and demanded money rent from the renter.
answer.turn: The owner no longer needed the grinding service and demanded cash; the renter insisted he would only grind as agreed.
answer.outcome: The passage leaves the dispute unresolved; no ruling is given in the passage itself.
answer.summary: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding done for him. He later grew rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and no longer needed the grinding, so he told the renter to pay money instead. The renter replied that he would grind as agreed but had not agreed to pay cash.
answer.missing: How the dispute was decided; the context only discusses it legally.

answer.actor: Rabbi Eliezer
answer.event: Rabbi Eliezer missed the study hall, met Rabbi Asi, asked what was said there, and heard that Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei.
answer.turn: Eliezer inferred from the ruling that only a single authority disagreed with Rabbi Yosei.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Asi confirmed with a baraita (in the context), but the anecdote serves a legal argument and has no real ending.
answer.summary: Rabbi Eliezer did not attend the study hall one day, so he asked Rabbi Asi, whom he met standing, what had been said. Asi reported Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Eliezer inferred that only one person must have disagreed, and Asi said yes, citing a baraita.
answer.missing: The anecdote is only a frame for a legal question; there is no real story arc.

answer.actor: A woman who seized a silver cup, and Rava
answer.event: A widow seized a silver cup against her marriage contract and also demanded sustenance, and brought the matter to Rava.
answer.turn: Rava dismissed the worry about Rabbi Shimon's view that part of a sum does not count as the whole.
answer.outcome: Rava ordered the orphan heirs to give her sustenance.
answer.summary: A woman took a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract and also asked for sustenance from the heirs. She went to Rava, who told the orphans to give her sustenance, since nobody follows Rabbi Shimon's view that part of the money is not treated like all of it.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could climb onto and off her bed using him as a step, and boasted of this in the study hall.
answer.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half of true honor, because he had not borne her throwing a purse into the sea in front of him without shaming her.
answer.outcome: He was deflated by the rebuke; no further outcome is stated.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend over so his mother could step on him to climb into and out of bed. He praised himself for this in the study hall, and the sages replied that he had not yet reached half of the honor due, since he had never faced her throwing his purse into the sea without embarrassing her.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Hanina and a man who kissed Yonatan's foot
answer.event: A man bent and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot as Yonatan and Hanina stood together, and Hanina asked why.
answer.turn: Yonatan explained the man had written his property over to his sons and Yonatan had forced the sons to feed him.
answer.outcome: The Gemara reads the story as showing that the law does not follow Rabbi Ile'a, because forcing the sons implies they were not obligated.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing together when a man came and kissed Yonatan's foot. Hanina asked what this was, and Yonatan said the man had given his property to his sons and Yonatan had made them feed him. The Gemara uses this to prove the law is not as Rabbi Ile'a held.

answer.missing: It describes Rav Huna's habitual practice of asking for a substitute worker before judging, not a single event with a turn and an ending.

answer.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava, and Rav Neḥemya
answer.event: A widow came before Rav Neḥemya and asked for sustenance and then wine, and he granted both.
answer.turn: He justified granting wine by the local custom of Mehoza residents drinking wine.
answer.outcome: She was awarded sustenance and wine.
answer.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Neḥemya and asked for sustenance, which he granted. She then asked for wine, and he granted that too, saying he knew the people of Mehoza drink wine.
answer.missing: It is a very short case report with only a slight turn.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef, who had forgotten his learning after illness, said he had never heard a halakha about roofs, and Abaye reminded him that he had taught it.
answer.turn: Abaye recounted what Yosef had said, which brought it back to Yosef's memory.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef recalled it and restated his teaching, correcting the version Abaye gave, and answered Abaye's follow-up challenge.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef, who had forgotten some of his learning, said he had never heard a certain ruling on roofs. His student Abaye said that Yosef himself had taught it, and recited it. Yosef then remembered and clarified what he had actually said, and answered Abaye's objection about residents.
answer.missing: Most of the passage is the legal content of the remembered teaching.
It is a question put to Rabbi Eliezer and his quip in reply; nothing happens beyond a question and answer.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called first his younger son Shimon and then his older son Gamliel and gave each his instructions.
answer.turn: He passed on wisdom to one son and the office of Nasi, with advice to rule firmly, to the other.
answer.outcome: Both sons received their transmission; the death itself is not within the text shown.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi neared death he asked for his younger son, Rabbi Shimon, and passed on the orders of wisdom to him. He then asked for his older son, Rabban Gamliel, gave him the procedures of the office of Nasi, and told him to lead firmly and cast fear on the students.
answer.missing: The beginning of the death narrative and its end are not in the passage.
It is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel; the case of Pishon the camel driver is only cited as a precedent, with no event told.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and two rival claimants to a field
answer.event: Two deeds on the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other just Nisan, and he awarded the field to the one with the specific date.
answer.turn: The losing claimant objected, and Rav Yosef pointed out his deed could be read as dated the twenty-ninth of Nisan.
answer.outcome: The loser asked for a document authorizing repossession, and the Gemara settles on both writing authorizations for each other.
answer.summary: Two buyers of the same field came to Rav Yosef, one with a deed dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the field to the specific date, and told the other his deed might be from the twenty-ninth. The loser asked for authorization to repossess later-sold property, Rav Yosef noted a flaw in that, and the Gemara proposed that they authorize each other.

answer.missing: It only reports how many blessings two sages recited at weddings; nothing turns or ends.
It is a chain of reported rulings by visiting sages on a legal question, with no story told.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and Abaye
answer.event: A person came before Rav Yosef, who told the heirs to give a daughter her sustenance from dates on mats, and Abaye objected.
answer.turn: Abaye pointed out that not even a creditor could collect from movable property.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef said he meant ripe dates still attached to the tree; the narrative ends as a legal exchange.
answer.summary: Someone came to Rav Yosef about a daughter's sustenance, and he told the sons to give it from dates laid on mats. Abaye objected that even a creditor could not collect that way. Rav Yosef answered that he meant dates still fit for mats, which are attached to the ground.
answer.missing: It is a short ruling and challenge exchange rather than a full story.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina and a poor man he supported
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars every Sabbath eve to a poor man, and one day his wife brought it and returned saying the man did not need it.
