answer.turn: Rava turned the oath over to the other party on his wife's word, but would not accept Rav Pappa's single testimony.
answer.outcome: Rava explained he trusted his wife because he knew her to be truthful, but did not have the same certainty about Rav Pappa.
answer.summary: A woman was ordered to take an oath before Rava, but his wife said she was untrustworthy about oaths, so Rava shifted the oath to the other side. Another time Rav Pappa told Rava a document had been paid, but Rava refused to rely on one witness. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Pappa was not trusted like Rava's wife, and Rava said he knew his wife was always truthful but lacked such certainty about Pappa.
answer.missing: Two separate incidents are combined in the passage.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: He once ruled in accordance with Rabbi Elazar's view about a woman's menstrual impurity.
answer.turn: Afterward he remembered that Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagree with him.
answer.outcome: He still said Rabbi Elazar may be relied upon in exigent circumstances.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once issued a ruling following Rabbi Elazar. Later he remembered that others disagreed with Rabbi Elazar. He nonetheless declared that Rabbi Elazar's view can be relied on in a pressing situation.

answer.actor: A steward appointed for a dead man's orphans, before Abaye
answer.event: A man had designated a field as a marker for another, contested it, and died; his steward came to Abaye, who said the deceased had forfeited his right.
answer.turn: The steward argued the father could have claimed he only meant one furrow, and then that he had bought the land back; Abaye accepted both claims.
answer.outcome: Abaye awarded the furrow with its palm trees to the orphans and praised the steward as the kind one should appoint.
answer.summary: A man who had marked a field as belonging to another later contested it and died, leaving a steward over his orphans. Abaye told the steward the right was lost. The steward argued that the father could have claimed he only gave one furrow, then that he had bought it back, and Abaye accepted each, giving the orphans the furrow with its palm trees. He said one should appoint a steward like this one.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar taught that the uneducated will not be revived; Rabbi Yohanan objected and Rabbi Elazar defended it from another verse.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar saw that Rabbi Yohanan was grieved for common people.
answer.outcome: He offered them a remedy: those who support Torah scholars are credited as cleaving to the Divine Presence.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan told Rabbi Elazar that God would not be pleased with his teaching that ordinary people will not be revived. Rabbi Elazar defended it with another verse. Seeing Rabbi Yohanan's distress, he offered a remedy: whoever marries his daughter to a scholar or supports scholars is counted as cleaving to God.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
answer.event: Several sages became impotent from Rav Huna's discourse, and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was afflicted by a disease of holding back urination.
answer.turn: They hung him from the cedar column of the study hall and a green substance came out of him.
answer.outcome: He was healed and said that of sixty elders he alone avoided the damage.
answer.summary: Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet became impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's discourse. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was afflicted too, but was hung from a cedar column and a green substance emerged, healing him. He said that of sixty elders he alone escaped.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
answer.event: Rabbi's first match for his son ended when the bride died; then his son married into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family after changing his plan to study first.
answer.turn: The bride's death made Rabbi fear a family flaw, and the son, seeing the new bride, switched from studying first to marrying first.
answer.outcome: Lineage was found sound (both from David's family); the son married, studied twelve years, and his wife who had become infertile was healed by prayer.
answer.summary: Rabbi arranged his son's match with Rabbi Hiyya's family but the girl died, so they checked the families' ancestry and found both descended from David's line. He then arranged a match with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, where the son, on seeing the bride, cut his planned study years and married first, ashamed before his father, who reassured him. After twelve years of study his wife was infertile and she was healed through prayer.
answer.missing: The passage joins two separate episodes; the ending of the second is in context segment [7].

answer.actor: Avimi, son of Rabbi Abbahu
answer.event: Avimi honored his father Rabbi Abbahu, running to open the door for him, and one day his father asked for water.
answer.turn: His father dozed off before he brought it.
answer.outcome: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke, and was rewarded with success in interpreting a psalm.
answer.summary: Avimi, already ordained with five sons, would run to open the door whenever his father Rabbi Abbahu knocked, calling out 'yes, yes'. One day his father asked for water and fell asleep before it came. Avimi stood bent over him until he woke, and was helped to interpret the psalm 'A song to Asaph'.

answer.actor: The orphans who divided the estate, and Rav Yosef and Abaye
answer.event: A man left a palm tree to his daughter, the heirs divided the estate without giving her one, and Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna.
answer.turn: Abaye distinguished the cases: the tree is held by all the heirs.
answer.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a tree and redivide the estate.
answer.summary: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the orphans divided the property and gave her none. Rav Yosef thought this was like the mishna's case. Abaye replied the cases differ because the tree is in the heirs' possession, and told them to give her a tree and divide again.
answer.missing: It is a legal case and ruling rather than an event with a human turn; the actual outcome is a recommended remedy, not a reported result.

answer.actor: A man who deposited pearls, before Rabbi Ami
answer.event: A man deposited seven pearls tied in a sheet in the house of Rabbi Meyasha, who died without instructions.
answer.turn: The family and the depositor came before Rabbi Ami in dispute over ownership.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled for the depositor because Meyasha was not wealthy and the man gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without saying whom they belonged to. The matter went to Rabbi Ami, who said Meyasha was not wealthy enough to own them and the claimant had given an identifying mark. He ruled the pearls belonged to the depositor.

answer.actor: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law, and the sages Ameimar, Mar Zutra, Rav Ashi and Rav Gamda
answer.event: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband while holding a garment, and three sages ruled she had lost her worn clothes.
answer.turn: Rav Gamda accused them of flattering Rav Zevid, since Rava had left the question unresolved.
answer.outcome: The conclusion: since it was not decided either way, what she seized is not taken from her, and what she did not seize is not given.
answer.summary: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband and held on to a garment. Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi ruled she had lost her worn clothes. Rav Gamda charged them with deferring to the great Rav Zevid, since Rava never resolved the point. The result was that she keeps what she seized and gets nothing she did not.

answer.actor: Ameimar
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for her one-tenth of the estate while her brothers said they would pay her off in cash if they had money.
answer.turn: Ameimar stayed silent at their remark.
answer.outcome: This was taken to show he retracted and treated her as a creditor.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi recounts standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers said that if they had money they would remove her by paying cash, and Ameimar said nothing. From his silence it was concluded he had retracted his view and held she was only a creditor.
answer.missing: The passage mainly states a legal opinion; the anecdote is brief and its point is inferred.

answer.actor: Nehemya, son of Rav Hanilai
answer.event: Nehemya was so absorbed in learning that he went out beyond his Shabbat limit.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman his student was in distress outside the limit.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman advised making a human partition so he could reenter.
answer.summary: Nehemya, deep in study, wandered beyond the Shabbat limit. Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman that his student was stranded and in distress. Rav Nahman said to form a wall of people for him to walk through and so return.

answer.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
answer.event: She immersed, and a bone was found between her teeth after she came up.
answer.turn: The bone showed an obstruction to the immersion.
answer.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
answer.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi's household immersed herself, and afterward a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi required her to immerse again.
answer.missing: The incident is cited only as a proof in a legal question; the passage itself is mainly argument.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
answer.event: After his wedding he went off and studied for twelve years.
answer.turn: On his return his wife had become infertile.
answer.outcome: He pleaded for mercy and she was cured.
answer.summary: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, and the son married and then spent twelve years in the study hall. When he came back his wife was infertile. Divorcing her or marrying another would have shamed her, so he prayed for mercy and she was healed.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar and Shmuel
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar doubted Rav Beruna's report of Shmuel's ruling and went to Shmuel to check.
answer.turn: Shmuel confirmed it, and Rabbi Elazar challenged him with Shmuel's own statement about the wording of the mishna.
answer.outcome: Shmuel was silent and did not answer.
answer.summary: Rav Beruna taught a ruling in Shmuel's name and Rabbi Elazar doubted it, so he had Beruna show him Shmuel's lodging. Shmuel confirmed the ruling to his face. Rabbi Elazar then objected that Shmuel himself had said the law follows the mishna's wording, and Shmuel just fell silent.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Ravina saw a man tie his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat and protested, but the man ignored him.
answer.turn: Ravina declared the man excommunicated in Rav Ashi's presence, then asked if that appeared irreverent.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him that where God's name is desecrated no honor is paid to a teacher.
answer.summary: While sitting before Rav Ashi, Ravina saw a man tie his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. He protested and was ignored, so he pronounced the man excommunicated. He then asked Rav Ashi whether that looked irreverent, and Rav Ashi said that when God's name is being profaned, one does not defer to a teacher.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar moved to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was seated on the calendar council, remarking at each step that he had been spared a curse.
answer.turn: Each milestone showed that one of three curses from Ezekiel's prophecy did not apply to him.
answer.outcome: He escaped all three curses.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was seated on the council of the calendar he said three. The verse in Ezekiel names these three as punishments for false prophets, and he avoided them all.
answer.missing: Little narrative action; mostly three remarks tied to a verse.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: They meant to act on a baraita letting a nursing mother remarry at once, but an old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it to her.
answer.turn: Rav Pappi showed from a baraita and Shmuel's rule that the stricter ruling applies; the two said they had not thought of it.
answer.outcome: They accepted it; the halakha was set that if the child died she may remarry, but if weaned she may not.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to permit a woman with a nursing child to remarry immediately, following a baraita. An old woman told them Rav Nahman had once forbidden it to her, and Rav Pappi argued from another baraita and a ruling of Shmuel that the restriction stands. They admitted they had overlooked it, and the final ruling was a compromise.

answer.actor: Ravina
answer.event: Ravina arranged his son's marriage and recited the wedding blessing from the betrothal, trusting the bride's family would not back out.
answer.turn: The bride's family retracted and the wedding was cancelled.
answer.outcome: His confidence proved wrong.
answer.summary: Ravina arranged a match for his son with the house of Rav Haviva and began reciting the wedding blessing from the betrothal, saying he was sure they would not retract. It did not work out and they retracted, so the wedding never happened.

answer.actor: Rav Safra and Rava
answer.event: Rav Safra objected to Rava that the Tigris separated Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than the permitted distance, so they should not count as one city.
answer.turn: Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the Tigris.
answer.outcome: The objection was answered: the cities were in fact linked.
answer.summary: Rav Safra challenged Rava, pointing out that a river separates the two cities that are treated as one. Rava took him outside and showed him the remains of a wall under the water that joined them, answering the challenge.

answer.actor: Ben Azzai
answer.event: His colleagues criticized Ben Azzai for teaching the duty to have children without marrying himself, and he answered that his soul yearned for Torah.
answer.turn: He defended himself by saying others can sustain the world.
answer.outcome: No change; he stayed unmarried.
answer.summary: The Sages told Ben Azzai that he preached procreation well but did not practice it. He replied that his soul was drawn to Torah and the world can be kept going by others.
answer.missing: A short exchange rather than a full event.

answer.actor: Rav Sheshet
answer.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons were his sons.
answer.turn: The Gemara explains he was merely putting them off, since he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses.
answer.outcome: His real reason was revealed, not a legal view.
answer.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry and father sons, and he replied that his daughter's sons count as his own. The Gemara says he was only deflecting them, because he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long lectures.
answer.missing: Brief anecdote embedded in legal argument.

answer.actor: A man who left a divorce condition and his arrival
answer.event: A man told agents holding his wife's get that it would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and he arrived at the end of the thirty days but was stopped by the ferry on the far side of the river.
answer.turn: He shouted across that he had come, but Shmuel said this was not a return.
answer.outcome: The condition was treated as unmet, so the get took effect.
answer.summary: A man gave a conditional divorce that would take effect if he did not come back in thirty days. He reached the river at the end of the period but the ferry was on the other side, so he called out that he had come. Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda and Rabba
answer.event: A divorce document dated by the governor of Bascar was sent by Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda to Rabba with a question.
answer.turn: Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it.
answer.outcome: The document was valid.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce had been dated by the years of the governor of Bascar. Rav Nahman sent it to Rabba to ask whether this was valid, and Rabba answered that even Rabbi Meir would allow it because the governor belonged to the same kingdom.
answer.missing: It is a legal query and reply; the case itself is barely told.

answer.actor: A man sent by his father to fetch chicks
answer.event: At his father's request he climbed to the roof, sent away the mother bird and took the young, thus doing two mitzvot.
answer.turn: On his way back he fell and died, though both mitzvot promise long life.
answer.outcome: The reward is understood to belong to the world to come.
answer.summary: A man's father told him to go up to a building and bring chicks. He climbed up, sent off the mother bird and took the young, and on the way down he fell and died. The question of where his promised long life went was answered by saying the reward is in the world that is entirely good.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
answer.event: Elders gathered in a loft in Lod were asked whether study or action is greater.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study, and then everyone agreed on study.
answer.outcome: They concluded study is greater because it leads to action.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in a loft in Lod when asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action and Rabbi Akiva answered study; all of them then agreed that study is greater since it leads to action.

answer.actor: Rabbi Akiva and his wife
answer.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter betrothed the shepherd Akiva and sent him to study, and her father disowned her.
answer.turn: Akiva returned after twelve years with thousands of students, then went off for twelve more at her urging; on his second return her father came to ask him to annul his vow.
answer.outcome: Her father learned who he was and gave Akiva half his money; the wife's recognition was honored.
answer.summary: Akiva was a shepherd when his employer's daughter saw his worth, betrothed him privately and sent him to study. Her father cut her off. Akiva came back after twelve years with twelve thousand students, overheard that she would be left alone, and went away for another twelve. He returned with twenty-four thousand students and she met him, and when her father came asking him to annul his vow, Akiva revealed himself and the father gave him half his money.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda
answer.event: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children, and he answered that if he had merited he would already have had them.
answer.turn: The Gemara says he was only putting them off, being impotent from Rav Huna's discourse.
answer.outcome: His real reason was revealed.
answer.summary: The Sages urged Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to remarry and have children and he said that if he had merited it he would already have had them. The Gemara explains he was deflecting them, because he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long lectures.
answer.missing: A short anecdote used only as a proof in a legal argument.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel and the sages Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok
answer.event: At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, Rabban Gamliel stood and served drinks to the sages.
answer.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup while Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Eliezer protested.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham and Rabbi Tzadok cited God to show that a leader may serve guests.
answer.summary: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok at his son's wedding. Eliezer would not take the cup and objected when Yehoshua did. Yehoshua pointed to Abraham serving his guests, and Tzadok said God Himself serves all, so Gamliel's serving was acceptable.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yosei
answer.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked how a wife helps a man.
answer.turn: Elijah answered with the example of raw wheat and flax that a wife turns into bread and clothing.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yosei was told that a wife lights his eyes and stands him on his feet.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yosei came across Elijah and asked what the verse means that a woman helps her husband. Elijah answered that a man brings home wheat and flax he cannot eat or wear raw, and his wife turns them into food and clothing.

answer.actor: A woman who gave her property to her daughter
answer.event: A woman about to marry wrote her property over to her daughter to keep it from her future husband, then was married and divorced.
answer.turn: She claimed the property back; Rav Nahman tore up the deed, Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva, and Mar Ukva said Shmuel too would tear such a document.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman's tearing of the deed was upheld.
answer.summary: A woman wrote her property over to her daughter so her husband could not reach it, then married and was divorced. She went to Rav Nahman, who tore up the document. Rav Anan complained about this to Mar Ukva, but after hearing the facts Mar Ukva said that Shmuel would also tear such a document of evasion.

answer.actor: A man who sold his property to ascend to Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: A man sold his property in order to go up to Eretz Yisrael but in the end did not go.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi gave a ruling on whether he can cancel the sale.
answer.outcome: The sale stood, with a version distinguishing cases of unavoidable obstacles.
answer.summary: A man sold his property with the intention of going to Eretz Yisrael but never went. Rav Ashi said that if he had wanted to he could have gone, so the sale stands, with a second version leaving room for the case where he was prevented on the way.
answer.missing: Case is only sketched; the passage is mostly about the ruling.

answer.actor: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
answer.event: For two and a half years the two schools disagreed over whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
answer.turn: They took a vote.
answer.outcome: They concluded it would have been better not to be created, but now he should examine his deeds.
answer.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued for two and a half years about whether man was better off created or not. They finally took a vote and decided it would be better not to have been created, but since he exists he should examine his actions.
answer.missing: A dispute and its resolution, not a story of individuals.

answer.actor: A dying man and Toviya
answer.event: A man told those at his bedside that his property should go to Toviya, then died, and Toviya came to claim it.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come.
answer.outcome: Toviya received the property.
answer.summary: A man said his property should go to Toviya and then died. When Toviya showed up, Rabbi Yohanan said that Toviya had come, meaning he gets the property.
answer.missing: The case is stated briefly; the ruling is the point.

answer.actor: Rava and the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami
answer.event: Rava forced Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity against his will.
answer.turn: A wealthy man was compelled to give though he had no particular obligation.
answer.outcome: Rava collected four hundred dinars from him for charity.
answer.summary: Rava once coerced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to donate to charity, and collected four hundred dinars from him. The incident is cited only as a precedent for forcing wealthy fathers to support their children, and it has no setup or reaction.
answer.missing: Why Rava acted, Rav Natan's reaction, and any background to the incident.

answer.actor: Rami bar Hama's sister and her husband Rav Avya
answer.event: Her marriage contract was lost and the couple went to Rav Yosef to ask what to do.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef answered with a ruling of Rabbi Meir that would make their marriage forbidden, and Abaye challenged it.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef conceded and told Rav Avya to go and write her a new marriage contract.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. They asked Rav Yosef, who answered by citing Rabbi Meir's strict view and the Sages' lenient one. Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir's decrees, and Rav Yosef told the husband to go write her a new contract.

answer.actor: The members of the house of the prince and the judges Rabbi Abbahu and colleagues
answer.event: The prince's household seized a maidservant of orphans for a debt, and the judges approved.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the powerful and noted that Reish Lakish had reversed a similar seizure.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba's rebuke leaves the approval in doubt, and the text shows no formal result.
answer.summary: The household of the prince seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley as payment for a debt. Rabbi Abbahu and the other judges said the seizure was good. Rabbi Abba asked whether they were flattering the prince's family, since Reish Lakish had overturned a similar act by judges who followed Rabbi Tarfon.
answer.missing: What the judges decided after Rabbi Abba's objection.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei
answer.event: He saw priestly gifts given directly to a priest's slave in Rabbi Yosei's locale, then testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's locale.
answer.turn: The court sought to elevate the slave to priesthood on his testimony, since in that locale eating teruma was taken as proof of priestly status.
answer.outcome: The attempt to elevate the slave did not go through.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei, said he testified only once in his life. He had seen a priest's slave receive teruma in his father's locale, where that proves nothing, and then testified to it in Rabbi Yehuda's locale, where it does. The court wanted to elevate the slave to priesthood on this basis, but in the end it did not.
answer.missing: How the elevation was stopped.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa
answer.event: He served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand up before him.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks to guests at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. He poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda, who did not stand before him. Rav Pappa became angry.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: He went up to Eretz Yisrael and was ordained and seated on the calendar council.
answer.turn: At each step he declared himself spared one more of the three curses in Ezekiel's verse.
answer.outcome: He escaped all three curses.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he joined the calendar council he said three. The three curses come from Ezekiel's verse about false prophets, and he escaped each.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat
answer.event: He betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat, and bystanders pointed out it was worth less than a peruta.
answer.turn: He said she could be betrothed with the four dinars hidden in the mat, and she took it and was silent.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled that her silence after the money was given counts for nothing.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat. People told him it was worth less than a peruta, so he said she was betrothed with the four dinars inside it. She took the mat and said nothing, and Rava ruled that silence after receiving the money proves nothing.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and Rav Beivai
answer.event: Rav Beivai told the Sages not to trust Rav Yosef's report of a teaching.
answer.turn: He said the teaching came from him in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, not from Rabbi, and Rav Yosef realized his mistake.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef exclaimed that he had confused the word Rabbi with the word rabbim.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef reported a ruling in the name of Rabbi. Rav Beivai told the Sages not to listen, saying he had given it to Rav Yosef himself in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, and the word was rabbim (many). Rav Yosef exclaimed in astonishment that he had mistaken one word for the other.

answer.actor: Rav Kahana
answer.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a seller of palm baskets.
answer.turn: He said he would go adorn himself, climbed to the roof and threw himself off, and Elijah caught him.
answer.outcome: Elijah gave him a basket of dinars, ending his need for the trade.
answer.summary: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, who sold palm baskets. He said he would go adorn himself, went up on the roof and fell. Elijah the prophet caught him and complained he had come four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana blamed his poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yirmeya
answer.event: A marriage contract was brought to Rabbi Abbahu, with the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature recognized.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abbahu thought to validate it, but Rabbi Yirmeya said the mishna requires the scribe to have signed.
answer.outcome: Not stated in the text.
answer.summary: A marriage contract came before Rabbi Abbahu. People recognized the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature, and he was inclined to validate it. Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the mishna requires the scribe to have signed.
answer.missing: Whether Rabbi Abbahu accepted the correction and what happened to the contract.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua
answer.event: He was asked about the rival wife of a daughter and about whose view is the law.
answer.turn: He refused to take sides between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, fearing for his skull.
answer.outcome: He instead testified that two great families, including High Priests, descended from rival wives.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua was asked about the rival wife of a daughter and whose view is the law. He said it was a dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel and asked why they were putting his head between two great mountains. He then testified that two great Jerusalem families, from which High Priests came, descended from rival wives.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
answer.event: Rav Aha visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda asked whether she might be betrothed, and each accused the other of violating a ruling of Rav or Shmuel.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha began to cite a justifying statement of Shmuel, which is completed in the next segment.
answer.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked if she might be betrothed, and Rav Aha replied that Rav Hisda had broken Rav's rule on betrothing minors. Rav Hisda answered that Rav Aha had broken Shmuel's rule against using a woman, and Rav Aha cited another saying of Shmuel, that all is for the sake of Heaven.
answer.missing: The passage is cut off mid-sentence; the end of Shmuel's quote is in the next segment, and no clear resolution is given.

answer.actor: Homa, Abaye's widow, and Rava
answer.event: Homa asked Rava for sustenance and wine, and while showing him the size of Abaye's cups her arm was uncovered.
answer.turn: Her beauty lit up the courtroom and Rava went home and asked his wife for intimacy.
answer.outcome: Rava's wife learned the cause and beat Homa with a chest lock until she was driven out of Mehoza.
answer.summary: Abaye's widow Homa asked Rava to set her sustenance and also wine. To show how large Abaye's cups were, she bared her arm, and her beauty lit up the courtroom. Rava went home and asked his wife for intimacy. His wife asked who had been in court, learned it was Homa, chased her out of Mehoza with a chest lock, and accused her of having already killed three husbands.

answer.actor: a woman who came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulders
answer.event: She raised the child she carried, and when he grew up he had intercourse with her.
answer.turn: They were brought to court on the presumption that he was her son, though that was not certain.
answer.outcome: The court stoned both of them, not because he was definitely her son but because he clung to her.
answer.summary: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child riding on her shoulders and raised him. When he grew up he had intercourse with her. They were brought to court and stoned, not because he was certainly her son but because he clung to her and so was presumed to be.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and a certain heretic
answer.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua as a man of thorns, citing a verse.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and sent him to read the rest of the verse, which turns the insult into praise.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua explained the verse as meaning that Israel's best protect it, like thorns sealing a breach, or grind the nations down.
answer.summary: A heretic told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya that a verse called Israel's best merely thorns. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse. He then explained that the best of Israel protect the people like thorns in a breach, or crush the nations.

answer.actor: Rabbi Meir
answer.event: Rabbi Meir, who used to mock transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and crossed a rope bridge toward her.
answer.turn: Halfway across, Satan dropped the disguise and said he would have destroyed Rabbi Meir but for the heavenly proclamation protecting him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Meir was spared only because of his standing in heaven, and was humbled.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir used to ridicule people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river. With no ferry, Rabbi Meir crossed on a rope bridge. Halfway over, Satan let him go and said that only the heavenly warning to be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah had saved him.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: A reservoir at Yavne thought to be full was measured and found deficient, so Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disagreed about the purifications already done in it.
answer.turn: They argued with parables and analogies, and Rabbi Akiva's argument that disqualification here is of the thing itself, like a blemished priest, prevailed.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon accepted Rabbi Akiva's reasoning and said that whoever separates from him separates from life.
answer.summary: A reservoir at Yavne was thought to hold the required amount but, when measured, was found short. Rabbi Tarfon would declare earlier purifications in it pure and Rabbi Akiva impure, and they argued with parables. Rabbi Akiva's analysis won, and Rabbi Tarfon conceded.
answer.missing: It is mostly a legal debate. The incident is only a framing, and nothing is said about the people who immersed.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Yeimar bar Hashu's agent seized a dead debtor's boat, and Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, who were also creditors, objected and then seized it themselves.
answer.turn: Each claimed to own the whole boat, and a third sage challenged whether they could acquire it that way.
answer.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese who strip people of their cloaks, since seizure after the debtor's death does not acquire anything.
answer.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told the agent that seizing it harmed other creditors, then seized the boat themselves and each claimed all of it. Rav Pineas objected and they came before Rava, who called them white geese who remove people's cloaks and said the seizure was invalid.

answer.actor: a certain woman and the man guarding an executed body
answer.event: A woman visiting her husband's grave had intercourse with a man guarding the body of someone executed by the king, and when that body was taken she proposed disinterring her husband as a substitute.
answer.turn: The body the guard was watching disappeared.
answer.outcome: She had her husband removed from his grave so the guard could claim he had done his job.
answer.summary: A widow visiting her husband's grave had intercourse with a man guarding the body of an executed man. When that body was taken, she suggested digging up her husband so the guard could say he had done his duty, and she removed him from his grave. The Rabbis cite it to show sin is possible even in mourning.
answer.missing: The Hebrew only alludes to the incident. The details come from the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, as seen by Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar saw the daughter gathering barley kernels from between horses' hooves in Akko.
answer.turn: She had once been very wealthy and was now reduced to scavenging.
answer.outcome: He applied a verse to her, reading it as saying she must follow the flock to sustain her body.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar swore he had seen Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter in Akko picking barley out of horse dung and hooves. He applied a verse about following the flock and read it as saying she must feed her own body from the leftovers.
answer.missing: This is an eyewitness report. How she fell from wealth is only implied by the surrounding discussion.

answer.actor: Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana
answer.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify about something Rav Ashi did not at first remember.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi eventually remembered and testified, and saw that Rav Kahana was hesitant, fearing he had put the testimony in his mind.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him he had not relied on him and had made the effort to remember the incident himself.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi knew of testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. When Rav Kahana asked whether he remembered it, Rav Ashi said no, and then said he did not know. In the end he remembered and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana hesitant, he said he had not relied on him but had remembered it by his own effort.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: They meant to permit a nursing mother to remarry at once, following a baraita, but an old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it to her.
answer.turn: Rav Pappi showed them from a baraita and a ruling of Shmuel that the stricter view applied.
answer.outcome: They admitted it had not been on their minds, and the ruling was set that remarriage is permitted if the child died and forbidden if she weaned him.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to act on a baraita letting a nursing mother remarry. An old woman said Rav Nahman had once forbidden it to her. Rav Pappi challenged them with another baraita and Shmuel's ruling, and they conceded they had forgotten it.
answer.missing: It is mostly legal argument, with only a thin episode of the sages being corrected.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman and a woman of Mehoza married in Neharde'a
answer.event: The woman and her husband came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and he noticed from her accent that she was from Mehoza.
answer.turn: He first ruled by the custom of Babylonia, following Rav, then was told she had married into Neharde'a.
answer.outcome: He reversed to rule by Shmuel's view, the custom of Neharde'a.
answer.summary: A woman from Mehoza who had married a man in Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. He heard her accent and ruled by the Babylonian custom, following Rav. When told she had married into Neharde'a, he ruled by Neharde'a's custom, following Shmuel.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Yehuda bar Mareimar
answer.event: Rav Pappa went to write his son's marriage contract with the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to greet him but would not go in.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa overcame Yehuda's reluctance to enter, since his presence would pressure Abba into a large dowry.
answer.outcome: Yehuda sat silent, Abba thought he was angry and wrote down all he owned as the dowry, then said he had left nothing for himself.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to greet him. At the door Yehuda hesitated to enter, and Rav Pappa pressed him until he went in and sat silent. The bride's father took his silence for anger and wrote all his property into the dowry, and then said he had left nothing for himself.

answer.actor: Reish Lakish, his disseminator Yehuda bar Nahmani, and the mourning Rav Hiyya bar Abba
answer.event: After Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child died, Reish Lakish went on the second day with his disseminator to comfort him and had him speak in turn.
answer.turn: The first words seemed to blame the dead child's generation, but are explained as saying Rav Hiyya was significant enough to be taken for the sins of the generation.
answer.outcome: The disseminator spoke on God's praise, the mourners, the comforters and all Israel, which are the blessings recited in a house of mourning.
answer.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child died. Reish Lakish did not visit on the first day. On the second he brought his disseminator and had him speak in turn on the dead child, God's praise, the mourners, those who comfort them and all Israel. The opening seemed to upset the mourner but meant he was important enough to be taken for the generation's sins.
answer.missing: The sequence of speeches has no dramatic ending and serves mainly to give the text of the blessings.

answer.actor: Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: Rabbi Akiva, who used to ridicule transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman at the top of a palm tree and began climbing it.
answer.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him and said that only the heavenly proclamation protecting Rabbi Akiva and his Torah saved him from ruin.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Akiva was spared, shown that he was not immune to temptation.
answer.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to mock people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he grabbed the trunk and began to climb. Halfway up, Satan dropped the disguise and told him he would have been destroyed were it not for a heavenly announcement to take care of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah.

answer.actor: A half-maidservant, half-free woman and her master
answer.event: The court forced the master of a half-maidservant to free her entirely.
answer.turn: The master was compelled to emancipate her.
answer.outcome: She became fully free.
answer.summary: Rav Huna bar Ketina reports in Rabbi Yitzhak's name an incident of a woman who was half slave and half free. The court forced her master to free her, and he made her a free woman. Only this bare result is given; the reason is argued over afterwards.
answer.missing: Who the people were, why the master was forced, and any scene; the passage only reports the outcome as a precedent.

answer.actor: A creditor and the herdsman of orphans' cattle, before Rav Nahman
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox of orphans, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive, while the herdsman said it was after death, and they came before Rav Nahman.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses and he had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that since the creditor could claim he bought it, he could equally claim he seized it during the debtor's lifetime, so the creditor's claim stood.
answer.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans' cattle. He said he seized it before the debtor died, and the herdsman said it was after. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses, and he had none, so Rav Nahman reasoned the creditor's claim must be accepted.

answer.actor: Mar Shmuel
answer.event: Mar Shmuel permitted his household to place a large mortar against the door to secure it.
answer.turn: He judged that the mortar counted as a utensil, so using it was not building.
answer.outcome: The mortar was allowed to be used as a door bolt.
answer.summary: In Mar Shmuel's house there was a large mortar. He allowed it to be set against the door to secure it, saying it had the status of a utensil.
answer.missing: This is a brief precedent case with a ruling rather than a story with a real turn or ending.

answer.actor: Mar Ukva
answer.event: Mar Ukva sent a pauper in his neighborhood 400 dinars every year on the eve of Yom Kippur, and one year sent them with his son.
answer.turn: The son came back saying the man did not need it because he saw them pouring old wine for him.
answer.outcome: Mar Ukva reasoned that a man so pampered needed more, and doubled the sum.
answer.summary: Mar Ukva yearly sent a poor neighbor 400 dinars before Yom Kippur. One year his son brought it and returned saying the man didn't need help, since old wine was being sprinkled for him. Mar Ukva concluded that someone used to such luxury needed even more, so he doubled the gift and sent it.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel and the people
answer.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives abandoned the dead and fled, until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel set a modest example.
answer.outcome: All the people followed, and even now plain burial garments are customary.
answer.summary: Funerals once cost relatives more than the death itself, to the point that they left the body and fled. Rabban Gamliel then arranged to be taken out for burial in plain linen, and everyone followed his example. Rav Pappa notes that people today bury even in cheap cloth.
answer.missing: A specific scene; it is a short account of a change in custom, not a single dramatized event.

answer.actor: Ravina
answer.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphan nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
answer.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine along.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
answer.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and also had his own wine to carry to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi if he could take the orphan's wine too, and Rav Ashi told him to go ahead, since the orphan's was no better than his own.

answer.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
answer.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
answer.turn: Wheat then arrived, making the sales unnecessary.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions be returned to their owners.
answer.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their former owners.

answer.actor: A beautiful woman
answer.event: A very beautiful woman, besieged by men wanting to betroth her, claimed to be already betrothed.
answer.turn: Later she betrothed herself to a man, and the Sages asked why.
answer.outcome: She explained she had said it to fend off unworthy suitors, and the Sages at Usha ruled that a statement with a rationale is believed.
answer.summary: A beautiful woman was pursued by many men and told them she was already betrothed. Later she betrothed herself to someone, and the Sages asked why. She said the earlier men were unworthy and the later one was worthy, and the Sages ruled she is believed since she gave a reason.

answer.actor: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya and Rav
answer.event: Rav Hinnana taught a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav before Rav in a wording that matched Rabbi Meir's stringent view.
answer.turn: Rav rebuked him for abandoning the Rabbis and following Rabbi Meir.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav Hinnana's reasoning and says the first clause follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Meir.
answer.summary: Rav Hinnana was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence and gave a wording matching Rabbi Meir. Rav asked him whether he had abandoned the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir.
answer.missing: Little event beyond a corrected teaching; the rest is legal explanation.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat so immersed himself in Torah that he studied in Tzippori's lower marketplace while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace.
answer.turn: One time someone came to take the cloak.
answer.outcome: He found a serpent on it guarding it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah that he sat studying in one marketplace of Tzippori and left his cloak lying in another. Once a person came to take it and found a serpent on it.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch, and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace, and Rav Aha bar Huna sent the question of what to do to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: The case was unclear since a myrtle branch might or might not be worth a peruta.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef replied to flog the man, as Rav would, and require a bill of divorce, as Shmuel would.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace. Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef, who replied to flog the man in line with Rav and also require a get in line with Shmuel, in case the branch was worth a peruta somewhere.

answer.actor: The Sages and Rav
answer.event: The Sages, faced with Shmuel's and Karna's conflicting statements, noted that Mar Ukva's court was nearby and also sent the question to Rav with the opinions' names reversed.
answer.turn: Rav swore that she needs both a get and refusal, and denied Shmuel would say otherwise.
answer.outcome: Rav ruled that she needs both.
answer.summary: When Karna challenged Shmuel's ruling as self-contradictory, the Sages suggested asking Mar Ukva's court nearby. They also switched the names and sent the question to Rav. Rav swore that she needs both a get and refusal and that Shmuel could not have said otherwise.
answer.missing: Who spoke to whom and the full setup of the test are only hinted at.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
answer.event: She brought the orphans to court to claim her marriage contract.
answer.turn: The orphans said it was demeaning for her to appear in house clothes, so she dressed in all her clothes.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled that the court appraises what a widow is wearing, so her clothes were counted against her marriage contract.
answer.summary: A widow was taking the orphans of her husband's house to court for her marriage contract. They told her it was shameful to go in plain clothes, so she put on all her clothes. Before Ravina, he ruled that the court appraises what a widow wears, so everything she had on was counted.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave, a gentile woman, Rav Yosef
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of intimate relations.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef said he could render her and her daughter fit to marry into Israel.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef's ruling is stated; its reasoning follows in the next segments.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of intimacy. Rav Yosef said he could treat both her and her daughter as fit to marry into the community.
answer.missing: The result is a ruling, and the reasons are in later segments; there is little narrative.

answer.actor: A man suffering from love for a woman
answer.event: A man in Eretz Yisrael was tormented over a certain woman and wanted to leave the land.
answer.turn: He heard the teaching about the great significance of living in Eretz Yisrael.
answer.outcome: He stayed in the land and suffered until his death.
answer.summary: Ilfa told of a man in Eretz Yisrael who suffered over a woman and sought to leave. When he heard the teaching about the merit of living in Eretz Yisrael, he stayed and endured it until he died.
answer.missing: The man is not named, and the story sits inside a letter to Rabba that is mostly advice.

answer.actor: A man claiming to be from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
answer.event: A man said he was from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and said Shot Mishot lies between the rivers.
answer.turn: Its location matters for lineage.
answer.outcome: The rest is discussion of why it matters and where the boundaries are.
answer.summary: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and pointed out that the place lies between the rivers, which bears on questions of lineage.
answer.missing: What happened to the man and the point of the remark; the passage turns into a boundary discussion.

answer.actor: Rav Anan
answer.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish while having a case before him, and Rav Anan said he was disqualified from judging his case.
answer.turn: The man explained the gift as a first-fruits-style offering to a scholar, so Rav Anan accepted it, then sent the man to Rav Nahman with a letter saying he was disqualified.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman, assuming the man was Rav Anan's relative, put aside an orphans' case to honor him, and the other litigant, seeing this, was cowed and lost.
answer.summary: A man with a lawsuit brought Rav Anan a basket of fish, and Rav Anan refused it and said he could not judge the case. The man said he wanted only to give the gift, citing the first-fruits teaching, and Rav Anan accepted, then sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified. Rav Nahman assumed the man was a relative, set aside an orphans' case to judge his, and the opponent was so cowed by the honor shown that he lost.

answer.actor: A Galilean woman
answer.event: A woman wanted to say to her friend 'come and I will feed you milk'.
answer.turn: Her imprecise speech made it come out as 'may a lioness eat you'.
answer.outcome: She said the wrong thing, showing the imprecision of Galilean speech.
answer.summary: A Galilean woman meant to invite her neighbor over for milk. Because of her imprecise pronunciation, what she actually said was 'may a lioness eat you'.

answer.actor: Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa (and Rav Ashi)
answer.event: Each recalls standing as waiter before a master who was served a fragrant dish.
answer.turn: The waiter craved the food and would have been endangered had he not been given some.
answer.outcome: The master gave him a share; the tellers draw a rule that aromatic or sharp foods must be shared.
answer.summary: Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa says he once stood before Mar Shmuel as a dish of mushrooms was brought, and he would have been endangered by craving had Shmuel not given him some. Rav Ashi tells a similar story about turnip slices in vinegar served to Rav Kahana. These are brief testimonies offered as evidence for a rule about sharing strongly flavored food.
answer.missing: Little detail of the scenes; the anecdotes serve a legal point.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ḥanina Kara
answer.event: While sitting before Rabbi Yannai he declared that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yannai rejected the ruling as wrong.
answer.outcome: Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses, since the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ḥanina Kara, a Bible reciter, sat before Rabbi Yannai and stated that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai sharply told him to go outside and recite his verses there, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: Rava taught that one may scatter straw on a rain-damaged courtyard on Shabbat, and Rav Pappa objected from a baraita.
answer.turn: Rava realized he had erred.
answer.outcome: He had a spokesman publicly announce that his earlier statement was a mistake and gave the correct rule.
answer.summary: Rava taught that on Shabbat one may spread straw on a courtyard ruined by rain. Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita requiring a different manner of scattering. Rava then appointed a spokesman and publicly announced that his earlier statement was his mistake, and gave the rule as taught in Rabbi Eliezer's name.

answer.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa, and Rav Pappa
answer.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen.
answer.turn: He ended up not needing the money and regretted the sale.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land, which the Gemara says was beyond the letter of the law.
answer.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed cash to buy oxen. In the end he did not need the money, and Rav Pappa gave the land back to him. The Gemara dismisses this as proof, since Rav Pappa acted beyond the strict letter of the law.

answer.missing: The passage is a halakhic and exegetical discussion of how girls' ripeness was known, not a narrative of events.
The passage reconstructs a hypothetical legal case about witnesses and a challenge, with no actual event.

answer.actor: A person who let witnesses trace their names on non-divorce documents, and Rav Kahana
answer.event: A person allowed witnesses to trace their names on other documents, not bills of divorce.
answer.turn: This went beyond the leniency allowed only for divorce bills.
answer.outcome: Rav Kahana ordered him flogged.
answer.summary: The leniency of having witnesses trace names written in saliva applies only to bills of divorce. One person nevertheless did this for other documents, and Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
answer.missing: Identity of the person and details of the incident.

answer.actor: A dying man and Toviya
answer.event: A man declared his property should go to Toviya and then died.
answer.turn: Toviya came to claim it, raising doubt whether another Toviya was meant.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yoḥanan said Toviya has come, so the property goes to him.
answer.summary: A man told those around him that his property should go to Toviya, and then he died. Toviya came to claim it, and Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled that Toviya had indeed come, so there was no need to worry about another Toviya.

answer.actor: Rav Kahana
answer.event: Rav Kahana held the beer of an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya, and delayed selling it until the Festival.
answer.turn: The beer might sour a little in the wait.
answer.outcome: He explained it would fetch cash at a better price at the Festival.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana was guardian of beer belonging to an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Ḥilkai. He held off selling it until the Festival, saying that although it might spoil a little, it would bring in real money then.

answer.actor: A man pining for a woman, as told by Ilfa
answer.event: A man in Eretz Yisrael, suffering over a woman, wanted to leave the land.
answer.turn: He heard the teaching about the great significance of living in Eretz Yisrael.
answer.outcome: He stayed and suffered there until the day he died.
answer.summary: Rabba's brothers wrote to him in Babylonia relaying Ilfa's story of a man who longed for a certain woman and wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael. When he heard the teaching about the importance of staying there, he remained and suffered until he died. The rest of the letter is advice urging Rabba to come.
answer.missing: Who the man and woman were and why leaving was connected to her; the rest of the passage is advice, not story.

answer.actor: A Madonite man in Jerusalem
answer.event: He wished to give away much movable property as a gift but could only do so by transfer through land.
answer.turn: He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and declared the gift together with the land.
answer.outcome: He died and the Sages upheld his words.
answer.summary: A man from Madon in Jerusalem had much movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him it could only be transferred together with land, so he bought a plot near Jerusalem and gave a portion of it to someone along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He died, and the Sages upheld his words.

answer.actor: Rava and a woman whose husband died in a famine
answer.event: A woman came before Rava and testified that her husband died in a famine.
answer.turn: Rava cross-examined her and she admitted he could not have survived on what she left, showing she did not see him die.
answer.outcome: Rava concluded famine is like war and retracted his earlier view.
answer.summary: Rava first thought famine differs from war for a wife's testimony of death. A woman then came and said her husband died in famine; Rava asked whether he could have survived on the little flour she left him, and she answered that he could not. Seeing she had not witnessed his death, Rava changed his ruling to treat famine like war.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi's daughter
answer.event: Ravina had Rav Ashi's daughter collect her one-tenth share from two estates.
answer.turn: From one son he gave intermediate land without oath, and from an orphan inferior land with oath.
answer.outcome: This is taken as proof she was treated as creditor of the sons.
answer.summary: Ravina arranged for Rav Ashi's daughter to collect her share from the estate: intermediate-quality land without an oath from Mar, and inferior-quality land with an oath from an orphan grandson. The Gemara reads this as evidence about whose creditor she was. It is a precedent report more than a story.
answer.missing: No real narrative arc; the account serves as legal proof.
